q: Which foreign traveler mentioned the development of the diamond industry in the Golconda region?
explanation: Marco Polo, who landed at Motupalli in Rudramadevi's reign, described the diamond mines of the Kakatiya (later Golconda) region. Abdur Razzaq and Domingo Paes wrote on Vijayanagara; Sir Thomas Roe on the Mughal court.

q: A foreign traveller who visited Andhra during the reign of Rudramadevi?
explanation: Marco Polo, the Venetian, visited Andhra (Motupalli) during Rudramadevi's reign and praised her rule and the prosperity of the kingdom. Domingo Paes and Nicolo Conti visited Vijayanagara; Jordanus was a missionary on the west coast.

notes.text: - **When:** visited in **Rudramadevi's** reign (DAO 2011; G2 2011 ×2; Group-II-A 1984) – reached the Coromandel coast in **1292**, towards the end of her reign.

q: In whose time did Marco Polo come?
explanation: Marco Polo came to Motupalli in the time of Rudramba (Rudramadevi), c. 1292. Option 'Rudramadeva' is a loose variant of the same queen's name, so the stem is loose; Rudramba is the standard form. Ganapatideva and Prataparudra are wrong.

notes.text: - **When:** visited in **Rudramadevi's** reign (DAO 2011; G2 2011 ×2; Group-II-A 1984) – reached the Coromandel coast in **1292**, towards the end of her reign.

q: Which foreign traveler visited Motupalli port during the Kakatiya period?
explanation: Marco Polo visited Motupalli c. 1292, towards the end of Rudramadevi's reign. Ibn Battuta, Abdur Razzaq and Nicolo Conti came later and elsewhere.

notes.text: - **Where:** landed at the Kakatiya port **Motupalli ("Mutfili")** (Group-I 1990-91; G1 1994; APPSC PYQ) – not Ibn Battuta, Abdur Razzaq, Nicolo Conti, Domingo Paes, Jordanus, Hiuen Tsang or Columbus.

q: Which Italian traveller visited Motupalli during the Kakatiya period?
explanation: The Italian (Venetian) Marco Polo visited Motupalli during Rudramadevi's reign and described it in his Travels. Nicolo Conti was also Italian but visited Vijayanagara in the 15th c.

notes.text: - **Who:** **Marco Polo**, the **Venetian (Italian)** traveller; work **Il Milione / The Travels**.

q: Kakatiya Pratapa Rudra was held captive by whom at the end of his life?
explanation: In 1323 Ulugh Khan (later Muhammad bin Tughlaq) captured Warangal and took Prataparudra II captive; he died on the way to Delhi. Malik Kafur (1309-10) only made him a tributary.

notes.text: - **Captor:** **Ulugh Khan** (Juna Khan, later **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**), under Sultan **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq** (APPSC G2 2019; G2 PYQ; Group-II-A 1989) – not Malik Kafur, Alauddin Khalji or Malik Chajju.

q: The Kakatiya King Pratapa Rudra became a captive at the end of his life to:
explanation: Prataparudra became a captive of Ulugh Khan (later Muhammad bin Tughlaq) in 1323. Alauddin never came south himself and Malik Kafur only made him a tributary.

notes.text: - **Captor:** **Ulugh Khan** (Juna Khan, later **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**), under Sultan **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq** (APPSC G2 2019; G2 PYQ; Group-II-A 1989) – not Malik Kafur, Alauddin Khalji or Malik Chajju.

q: The person who defeated Prataparudra-II and took him captive?
explanation:
Key: Ulugh Khan (the usual name in keys). Juna Khan, also printed, is the same man (Muhammad bin Tughlaq), and NextGen Kakatiyas p.59 uses that name, so both options are strictly right.
In the final invasion of 1323 Ulugh Khan (Prince Juna Khan, later Muhammad bin Tughlaq) defeated Prataparudra II and took him captive; he died on the Narmada on the way to Delhi. Malik Kafur's 1309-10 siege ended in a treaty.

notes.text: - **Captor:** **Ulugh Khan** (Juna Khan, later **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**), under Sultan **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq** (APPSC G2 2019; G2 PYQ; Group-II-A 1989) – not Malik Kafur, Alauddin Khalji or Malik Chajju.

q: After the victory in 1323, the Delhi Sultans changed the name of Warangal to?
explanation: After capturing Orugallu in 1323, the Tughlaqs renamed Warangal Sultanpur. The other names are distractors.

notes.text: - **Renaming:** Orugallu → **Sultanpur** (APPSC PYQ).

q: In which year did Kakatiya kingdom fall?
explanation: The Kakatiya kingdom fell in 1323 when Ulugh Khan took Warangal. 1313 and 1318 were tributary treaties; 1336 is the founding of Vijayanagara.

notes.text: - **Year:** **1323** – the end of the Kakatiya kingdom (Group-II-B 1989); final siege about **five months**; **Bobbareddi's** withdrawal weakened the defence.

q: Which king introduced the Nayankara system during Kakatiya rule?
explanation:
Book key: Rudramba (a NextGen Level-II line says 'implemented by Rudrama'). Most books, NextGen's administration chapter and the APPSC 2025 statement question: Prataparudra (II) introduced/reorganised it into 77 Nayankaras.
The Nayankara system - military officers (Nayakas) holding Sthalas and forts for a fixed tribute - was introduced by Prataparudra II, who organised the kingdom into 77 Nayankaras. Nayakas served earlier rulers, but the system is credited to Prataparudra.

notes.text: - **Golusukattu cheruvulu** = linked **chain tanks**; **Dashabandhamu** = tax-free land for tank upkeep.

q: Which doctrine gave birth to the Kapalikas?
explanation:
Most book keys: Pasupata Saivism. NextGen's PYQ list (AP History 06; Powerplay #1 6.1) records 'Misra Saivam' (option 3).
The Kapalikas, like the Kalamukhas, are counted as an extreme offshoot of the old Pasupata (Lakulisa) Shaivism – Ramanuja classes them all as Pasupatas. Vaishnavism and Suddha Saivam are unrelated.

notes.text: - **Kapalikas emerged from:** **Pasupata Shaivism** (APPSC G2 2019; APPSC PYQ).

q: In which text of the Kakatiyas can we find the legal principle that "a woman's property inherits perfectly to her daughters and to her daughter's daughter"?
explanation: The tenet comes from Ketana's Vignanesvaram, the Telugu rendering of the Mitakshara; Sivadevayya's Purushartha Saramu deals with polity (72 Niyogas), not inheritance. (Printed key Purushartha Saramu was wrong.)

q: Women's property is inherited wholly by the daughters and the daughter's daughters * " — In which work of the Kakatiya period can we find this legal tenet?
explanation: Ketana's Vignanesvaram (Telugu Mitakshara) states that a woman's property passes wholly to her daughters and daughters' daughters; the other three are polity texts.

notes.text: - **Decline of Jainism:** **Kalamukha and Veerashaiva hostility**; Jain–Saiva conflicts from Rudradeva's reign.

q: In which district is the Ramappa temple located?
explanation:
Mulugu district was carved out of Jayashankar Bhupalpally (ex-Warangal) in Feb 2019 — now Palampet is in Mulugu district, Telangana (UNESCO WHC 1570; Telangana GO 2019)
Palampet (Ramappa) was in Warangal district (now Mulugu district, Telangana).

notes.text: - **District:** **Warangal** in the books (APPSC PYQ) – now **Mulugu**.

q: The famous Kakatiya Temple (Ramappa) at Palampet was built in?
explanation: Recherla Rudra, general of Ganapatideva, built the Ramappa (Rudreswara) temple at Palampet in 1213. 1162-63 is the Thousand Pillar temple.

notes.text: - **Year:** **1213** (G1 1990-91; G1 1994) – 1162 is the Thousand Pillar temple.

q: Builder of the thousand-pillared temple in Hanumakonda
explanation: Rudradeva (Prataparudra I) built the Rudreswara or Thousand Pillar temple at Hanumakonda in 1162-63. Ganapatideva, Rudramadevi and Prataparudra II came later.

notes.text: - **Builder:** **Rudradeva / Prataparudra I** (G1 1991; G2 2011 ×2; Geologist 2007; APPSC PYQ ×2) – not Ganapatideva, Rudramadevi or Prataparudra II.

q:
Which of the following statements regarding Kakatiyas are correct?
I. Early Kakatiya monarchs had constructed Jain temples.
II. The influence of Chalukya temple architecture could be seen in Kakatiya temples.
III. Thousand pillared temple was built in ' Trikuta style ', having three shrines, each dedicated to Rudreshwara, Vasudeva and Suryadeva.
explanation: II and III are correct – Chalukyan (Kalyani) influence and the Trikuta plan with Rudreswara, Vasudeva and Surya. Statement I is not accepted: the Jain basadi at Anumakonda was built by minister Chetana's wife Mailama, not by the monarchs (APPSC key).

notes.text: - **Statements (G2):** Chalukyan influence ✓; Trikuta with Rudreswara, Vasudeva, Suryadeva ✓; "early Kakatiya **monarchs** built Jain temples" ✗ (the Jain basadi was a minister's wife's) → **II and III only**.

q: The royal preceptor of Ganapatideva was
explanation: Visvesvara Sambhu (Visvesvara Shivacharya of the Golaki matha) was the diksha-guru (royal preceptor) of Ganapatideva, as the Malkapuram inscription records. Panditaradhya was an Aradhya Shaiva teacher; Basava founded Veerashaivism.

notes.text: - **Ganapatideva's royal guru (preceptor):** **Visvesvara Sambhu** (G1 1983-84; G1 1984; APPSC PYQ) – not Basava, Panditaradhya or Narahari Tirtha.

q: As per which inscription, Rudramadevi's death during an expedition to the South in 1289 AD was confirmed?
explanation: The Chandupatla inscription (Nalgonda), set up by Puvvula Mummadi, records Rudramadevi's death in 1289 while fighting Kayastha Ambadeva.

q: Which inscription mentions the musical instrument "Jalakaranda"?
explanation: The musical instrument Jalakaranda is mentioned in the Kakatiya Dharmasagar (Dharmasagaram) inscription.

notes.text: - **Jalakaranda:** **Dharmasagar** (G2 2011 ×2; G2 PYQ; APPSC PYQ) – not Chebrolu, Malkapuram, Pillalamarri, Porumamilla or Warangal fort.
